extracted.intended_audience: scholars and researchers in journalism/media studies; media professionals interested in influences on news content (especially television news)
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing and modeling how various external and internal forces (extramedia, organizational, within-media) affect television news content and coverage decisions, using survey measures (reporters' perceptions) and structural modeling. Includes measurement choices and hypothesized causal paths among constructs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market Size (DMA, reverse-coded)
rubrics_metrics.description: Market size defined by reverse-coding respondents' designated market areas (DMAs); larger DMA ranks represent larger markets after reverse-coding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originally proposed as a control variable with a predicted negative effect (smaller-market respondents would report more influences on content due to poorer resources, smaller staffs, stronger advertiser pressure). Exploratory testing found no direct effect on overall influences; instead, market size had a stronger, direct negative influence on the Extramedia Influences construct (reporters from smaller DMAs perceived more extramedia pressures), and thus an indirect effect on overall influences via other constructs. Reverse-code DMAs for clarity when larger ranks should indicate larger markets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extramedia Influences
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct measured by pressures from advertisers, public relations practitioners, and political/government officials (forces outside the media).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpreted as pressures originating external to news organizations (advertiser, PR, political pressures). Hypothesized to affect Organizational and Within-Media influences; exploratory testing showed Extramedia has a direct effect on Organizational Influences and an indirect effect on Within-Media (mediated by Organizational pressures). Treat as endogenous or exogenous depending on model placement (note: changing Market Size location changed Extramedia from exogenous to endogenous in this study).

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational Influences
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct represented by three measures: economic pressures, owner/top-level executive pressures, and staff size pressures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originally modeled to covary with Extramedia Influences; exploratory model testing supported a direct path from Extramedia to Organizational Influences. Organizational influences were found to directly affect Within-Media Influences and also to have a direct relationship with overall Content Influence/Outcome (i.e., reporters may self-censor or self-edit without managerial direction). Consider including ownership concentration as an Organizational indicator in future work (omitted here due to low reliability).

rubrics_metrics.name: Within-Media Influences
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct measured by direct and indirect pressures from newsroom management (pressures within the news organization).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functions as the main mediator in the IOMC model: Extramedia and Organizational pressures pass through Within-Media before affecting Influences/Outcomes on Content. Model testing suggested Extramedia affects Within-Media primarily indirectly via Organizational pressures, not directly. Within-Media was operationalized using two measures (direct and indirect management pressures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Influences and Outcomes on Content and Coverage Decisions (Main Dependent Variable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measured by reporters' perceptions of (1) agenda building, (2) frame building, and (3) agenda cutting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three outcome indicators capture how influences manifest in news content: agenda building (which topics get placed on the news agenda), frame building (how topics are presented/framed), and agenda cutting (which topics are kept off or removed). Within-Media Influences were directly related to increases in these content influence measures. Use reporters' perceptions to assess instances of these outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct Management Pressures (Within-Media indicator)
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct pressures assessed by survey questions asking how often newsroom managers/superiors 'provide clear instructions or directly tell reporters what to cover, how to cover it, or what not to cover.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat as an indicator of overt managerial control. Direct pressures are distinct from indirect pressures and were measured separately. Useful for assessing explicit managerial directives that influence coverage decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect Management Pressures (Within-Media indicator)
rubrics_metrics.description: Indirect pressures involve subtle means such as yawning at or making fun of a story idea, showing disinterest by not airing a reporter's story, or other covert signals that socialize journalists over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Considered powerful but historically understudied because of measurement difficulties; the study operationalizes indirect pressures through concrete vignette-style behaviors. Recognize that repeated indirect signals can lead to 'osmosis' socialization where reporters self-edit. Include clear examples when measuring (e.g., yawn, ridicule, ignoring) to improve reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staff Size Pressures
rubrics_metrics.description: Measured by two survey questions assessing reporters' opinions on an inadequate or reduced staff size and its effects on news coverage (questions ask about TV stations in general, not the respondent's station).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as an Organizational Influences indicator here (re-classified from Within-Media because it associated more strongly with Organizational factor). Staff size pressure was positively correlated with public relations pressures and with Overall Influences on News Content. When designing measures, ask about industry/general perceptions to elicit more candid responses. Note: the indicator assesses perceptions of effects, not objective staffing levels at a respondent's station.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertiser Pressure (Extramedia measure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pressure from advertisers to favor content that presents them positively or to avoid content that might offend advertisers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically found to succeed more in smaller markets. Use scenarios or ethics vignettes to measure likelihood of bowing to advertiser demands. Consider linkage to economic pressures at Organizational level in modeling (advertiser pressure contributes to perceived economic constraints).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public Relations Pressure (Extramedia measure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Influence exerted by public relations practitioners via information subsidies and other tactics to shape news coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positively correlated with staff size pressures (smaller staffs increase use of information subsidies). Measure through frequency/impact of PR-provided materials and reporters' reliance on such subsidies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political/Governmental Pressure (Extramedia measure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pressure from political officials or government actors that can influence coverage decisions (e.g., complaints, demands, or official expressions of displeasure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include governmental response examples (e.g., national embarrassment, diplomatic/economic reactions) when measuring. Can link directly to Organizational responses (e.g., corporate owner interests) as shown in examples like NBC-China apology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic Pressure (Organizational measure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Perceived financial pressures affecting news organizations (pressure to protect financial interests of owners/advertisers/investors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalize via perceptions that stories that would harm financial interests are avoided; relates to owners'/investors' influence. Economic pressure was found to mediate effects from Extramedia to Within-Media and to influence content decisions directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Owner/Top-Level Executive Pressure (Organizational measure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Perceived pressure from owners or top-level executives to shape news coverage, including protecting corporate interests or relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure perceptions that owners exert influence on story selection or tone; evidence and anecdotes (e.g., executives on corporate boards) can justify expecting a direct influence on newsroom management and content. Can produce direct effects on content (self-censorship by reporters) as well as via Within-Media pressures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respondent Selection and Question Framing (Methodological criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose reporters (rather than news directors) as survey respondents and ask about TV stations in general to obtain more candid responses about industry pressures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: reporters are more removed from business side and more transient, thus less likely to cater answers to protect their organization. Asking about the industry in general reduces offense and increases candor when questions involve sensitive topics (e.g., pressures exerted by colleagues). Use this design choice when the goal is candid perception data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ownership Concentration (proposed Organizational indicator; omitted)
rubrics_metrics.description: An ownership concentration index was considered as an Organizational indicator but exhibited low reliability with other variables and was omitted from the model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider refining the ownership concentration measure in future research; if reliable, include as an Organizational-level predictor of Within-Media and Content influences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agenda Building / Frame Building / Agenda Cutting (content influence sub-measures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three distinct content outcomes: agenda building (inserting topics onto news agendas), frame building (constructing presentations/interpretations of topics), and agenda cutting (keeping topics off or removing them from coverage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as separate dependent indicators to capture different ways influences manifest in content. Agenda cutting is specifically measured as self-censorship or avoidance of newsworthy stories; prior survey evidence (Pew) can be used for comparative validation.
